name: Online News Outlets
description: Online reporting about Iran connects domestic institutions, journalists abroad, and readers whose access to information can change during internet restrictions. Understanding an outlet requires examining its funding, reporting methods, and ability to verify events inside the country.[s1][s2]

seo.title: Online News Outlets Covering Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Persian-language online reporting, funding disclosures, exile journalism, and the verification problems created by internet shutdowns.

content.heading: Reporting across borders
content.content:
Reporting about Iran is produced both inside the country and by journalists working abroad. Physical distance does not necessarily remove a newsroom from its sources, but communication restrictions can abruptly weaken those relationships. In interviews published by the Reuters Institute in February 2026, journalists in exile described the difficulty of checking events during the shutdown that began on 8 January. Their accounts establish the reporting conditions they experienced at that time; they do not establish conditions throughout the rest of 2026.[s1]

The interviews identify an important distinction between publishing capacity and reporting access. A newsroom abroad may retain its website and editorial staff while losing contact with people inside Iran. Consequently, the continued appearance of articles does not, by itself, demonstrate that reporters can independently confirm every development on the ground.[s1]

content.heading: Institutional identity and editorial claims
content.content:
Radio Farda illustrates why an outlet's institutional identity should accompany its coverage. Its Persian-language information page identifies it as the Iran service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, funded by the United States Congress and operating under the US Agency for Global Media. It also states an ambition to provide accurate, objective, impartial reporting to Persian-speaking audiences. The funding description and the editorial ambition are different kinds of information: the first describes an institutional arrangement, while the second describes the organization's stated standards.[s2]

Its English-language introduction explains that the English site offers selected coverage of Iran's economy, domestic politics, and international affairs from Farda and RFE/RL. International readers should therefore distinguish a selected English service from the complete Persian-language output. An English article can be useful without representing everything the newsroom publishes for its principal audience.[s3]

content.heading: Reading for evidence
content.content:
A practical reading method starts with the article rather than the outlet's reputation alone. Identify whether a claim comes from an official announcement, an eyewitness, a document, or the journalist's analysis. Follow links to the underlying material when available, and distinguish independent corroboration from several sites repeating the same original account. These are editorial reading principles, rather than a ranking of the organizations discussed here.

The distinction becomes particularly valuable during communication failures. The Reuters Institute's interviewees described using trusted relationships, diaspora networks, satellite imagery, and open-source verification, while also explaining how the loss of contact restricted what they could establish. Those methods should be assessed claim by claim; their availability does not guarantee that every image or testimony has been verified.[s1]

This page is an introduction to those distinctions, rather than a comprehensive directory. A fuller account requires separately verified profiles of domestic agencies, commercial and specialist publications, regional reporting, and additional outlets operating abroad.

name: Social Media
description: Iran's social-media environment is shaped by the difference between a platform's formal restrictions and its actual reachability on particular networks. Reporting and technical measurements document changes in access, while also showing why a single nationwide label can conceal important differences.[s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Social Media and Platform Access in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore documented changes in platform access in Iran and the differences between policy announcements, filtering, and internet shutdowns.

content.heading: Access is more than a platform label
content.content:
For readers encountering Iran's digital environment, terms such as blocked, available, and popular require care. A government decision to remove a restriction does not necessarily mean that every user immediately obtains access. Conversely, blocking does not demonstrate that nobody uses a service. Associated Press reporting on the December 2024 removal of restrictions on WhatsApp and Google Play recorded differing experiences on computers and mobile phones, alongside the use of proxies and virtual private networks to reach restricted services.[s1]

Messaging and public social publishing should also be distinguished. WhatsApp can carry private conversations, while a public video platform exposes material to a different audience. Grouping every service under social media can obscure what a restriction prevents: private contact, public distribution, or both.

content.heading: A documented sequence of changes
content.content:
On 24 December 2024, Associated Press reported that Iran's Supreme Council of Cyberspace had lifted restrictions on WhatsApp and Google Play. This was a specific decision concerning named services, rather than evidence that all platform restrictions had ended.[s1]

The Open Observatory of Network Interference, or OONI, subsequently examined WhatsApp connectivity. Its August 2025 finding states that measurement results corroborated the December unblocking, but also identified renewed anomalies between 15 June and 12 July 2025. OONI interpreted these results as evidence suggesting interference on some Iranian networks during and after the June conflict with Israel. It did not describe every anomalous test as definitive proof of a nationwide block.[s2]

Freedom House's 2025 assessment separately described extensive website filtering and restrictions on major social platforms. Its principal reporting period ran from June 2024 through May 2025, with additional discussion of the June conflict. That period matters: an annual report's title should not be mistaken for continuous observation through the present.[s3]

content.heading: What measurements can establish
content.content:
OONI's investigation distinguished service interference from a general loss of connectivity. Some tests established network connections but failed during the encrypted connection handshake. The researchers also compared results with WhatsApp reachability elsewhere, reducing the likelihood that a global service outage explained the Iranian anomalies. These distinctions give a more precise account than simply saying that the internet was unavailable.[s2]

Restrictions also have consequences beyond loading a particular application. Freedom House documented surveillance and punishment connected to online expression during its reporting period. Technical access and freedom to speak are therefore separate questions: a person may reach a platform while facing serious consequences for using it.[s3]

For interpreting future reports, ask which service was tested, on which networks, during which dates, and with what uncertainty. A policy announcement, a technical test, and a user's experience illuminate different aspects of access. None should automatically substitute for the others.[s1][s2] A complete account of social media additionally needs evidence about everyday cultural exchange, commerce, domestic platforms, and differences among communities; the sources inspected here do not adequately cover those subjects.

name: Persian Podcasts
description: Persian-language podcasts include narrated nonfiction, book explanations, and accounts of lived experience. Channel B, Bplus, and Radio Marz illustrate distinct editorial approaches, although their catalogs do not establish the size or composition of the wider listening public.[s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Persian Podcasts: Stories, Books and Experience | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover contrasting approaches to Persian audio through Channel B, Bplus, and Radio Marz, with guidance on sources, formats, and listening.

content.heading: Different kinds of listening
content.content:
Persian podcasts offer several ways into a subject: following a carefully constructed story, encountering the argument of a nonfiction book, or listening to accounts of social experience. These approaches are visible in the publisher descriptions and catalogs of Channel B, Bplus, and Radio Marz. They are useful examples of editorial variety, rather than a ranking or a representative census of Persian audio.[s1][s2][s3]

For an international reader, Persian-language publishing should not automatically be equated with an audience located entirely inside Iran. The inspected pages describe programs and production, but do not establish where all their listeners live. Language, subject matter, production location, and audience geography are separate questions.

content.heading: Channel B: constructing an audio narrative
content.content:
Channel B's own history dates its first episode to summer 1394 in the Iranian Solar Hijri calendar. It describes an initial project telling true stories, launched with assistance from Namlik, that gradually developed into a team production. Ali Bandari is identified as its founder and narrator.[s1]

The team's description reveals work that can disappear behind a recognizable voice. Editing and sound design involve arranging recorded speech, selecting music, and shaping the audio narrative. Other responsibilities include artwork, technical maintenance, release management, and financial administration. A podcast can therefore be a collaborative editorial production even when listeners mainly recognize its narrator.[s1]

Channel B also distinguishes free listening from permission to republish. Its information page says episodes are free to hear, while republication of the podcast or its text requires permission. Accessibility to listeners should not be interpreted as an unrestricted reuse license.[s1]

content.heading: Bplus: introducing books and ideas
content.content:
Bplus describes its podcast as Persian summaries of nonfiction books. Its Acast catalog credits writing, narration, and editing separately for book episodes, making the editorial stages visible. A summary is best approached as an introduction to an author's argument: selection and compression necessarily shape what the listener encounters.[s2]

The same feed also contains broader explanatory productions, including material about the Caucasus and Saudi Arabia. Some descriptions supply reading links and separate credits for script and audiovisual production. This makes the feed a useful example of the overlap between an audio program and a wider digital publishing project. Readers should inspect each episode's description to establish its format and underlying sources rather than assuming every entry is a book summary.[s2]

content.heading: Radio Marz: experience and social distance
content.content:
Radio Marz's catalog takes another approach, organizing episodes around experiences that create distance between people. Entries published before the editorial cutoff address job loss, online harassment of women, expectations of masculinity, and political estrangement among people close to one another. The descriptions foreground personal accounts rather than presenting these subjects as statistical surveys.[s3]

That distinction matters when listening. An account may reveal how a situation feels, what language people use to explain it, and which relationships it strains. It does not by itself establish how common that experience is across Iran. The catalog also identifies sponsors for some episodes; sponsorship disclosure is part of understanding the production context.[s3]

Across these examples, a productive starting point is to ask what an episode promises: a narrative, an explanation of a published argument, or testimony. Then examine its credits and references. The reward is a more precise understanding of both the subject and the editorial choices that brought it to the listener.[s1][s2][s3]
